source.title: The nuclear route: sharp asymptotics of ERM in overparameterized quadratic networks
source.authors: Vittorio Erba; Emanuele Troiani; Lenka Zdeborová; Florent Krzakala

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives and numerically illustrates ERM test-error learning curves for quadratic networks, bearing on sample-wise double descent and model-width dependence. It uses an analytical asymptotic method rather than reproducing the original studies' methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a sample-complexity sweep with a test-error cusp near interpolation and states that the cusp emerges as regularization decreases. It also states that, with appropriately matched regularization, test error is independent of student width for κ ≥ 1. Double-descent results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: An analytical (replica/AMP) characterization of ERM learning curves in two-layer quadratic networks, a new setting. It yields a sample-wise test-error peak at the interpolation threshold (α=n/d²) that grows as λ→0+ in the noisy case, plus a width-invariance result for κ≥1. Double descent is a side result here, not the paper's aim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The main contribution is mapping ℓ2-regularized ERM in quadratic networks to nuclear-norm matrix sensing, yielding sharp asymptotic train/test errors, interpolation and strong-recovery thresholds, and a low-rank limit. Double descent appears only as a remark: in the noisy case a cusp develops at the interpolation threshold as λ decreases. Results are width-independent for κ≥1 with rescaled regularization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies synthetic teacher-student quadratic networks using high-dimensional asymptotic analysis of regularized ERM, with finite-size numerical comparisons; it does not reproduce the original studies' methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The sample-wise cusp is reported as regularization decreases; the curves also vary with label-noise level and regularization. Width invariance is stated for κ ≥ 1 when regularization is appropriately matched.

fits_no_version.finding: The interpolation threshold, and so the location of the sample-wise peak, depends on target width κ* and label noise Δ, not on the student's parameter count or width. Interpolation can occur well before α=1/2 when the target is narrow (Result 1, Eq. 13).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The peak location is set by a data- and target-dependent capacity (the largest number of samples the model can fit), not by the raw ratio of parameters to samples.

record.problems: The main findings concern synthetic Gaussian-input, single-hidden-layer quadratic networks in a high-dimensional limit. The text identifies finite-size numerical comparisons, but the learning curves in Figure 3 provide no stated uncertainty estimates.

untested.parts: Model-wise curve across the capacity threshold (κ<1 students); deep networks; fixed (unmatched) regularization across widths.
Epoch-wise curves are not studied; only global minima at convergence are analysed.
Real data, deep architectures and other model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested across size, epochs and samples.

Multiple or triple peaks. Whether optimal regularization removes the peak is not stated. Noise dependence is shown only by contrasting the Δ=0 and Δ=0.5 figures, which the text does not describe as presence versus absence of a peak.
No recounting of effective parameters to turn the second descent into a U-shaped curve.

missing.what: Without the PSD constraint (arbitrary-sign second layer), the test error diverges at the interpolation peak α=0.5 for κ*=0.2, Δ=0.5, λ→0+. The peak shrinks as λ grows.
Noiseless (Δ=0) learning curves for λ=0.4, λ→0+ and optimal λ, which the text does not describe as having a cusp. Strong recovery occurs before the interpolation threshold (Fig 4 center).
Analytic interpolation-threshold formula and limits (α_inter→1/4 as Δ→∞; (1+2κ*−κ*²)/4 for Δ→0, κ*<1), giving the peak location as a function of noise and target width.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is a theoretical analysis in a new model class whose aim is not double descent. It is a shallow two-layer network, so V1's 'deep networks' framing only loosely applies. The V1 verdict is limits_scope, not challenges, because the width-invariance regime lies entirely past capacity saturation and never spans a would-be peak. The V6 regularization evidence is figure-based plus the authors' one-sentence description.

versions.untested_parts: Width dependence is addressed for quadratic networks with κ ≥ 1 and appropriately matched regularization; other architectures and width regimes are not tested.
Test error over training epochs is not measured as a learning curve.
The reported peak is for the studied synthetic quadratic-network setting; other models and data settings are not tested.
The paper studies quadratic networks, not double descent across multiple model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across axes.

The paper shows a regularization-dependent cusp in a noisy setting. It does not test multiple or triple peaks, and the effect of optimally tuned regularization is not explicitly characterized in the text.
The paper does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that removes the second descent.

rows.subject: two-layer quadratic neural network (ERM)
rows.operation_detail: Compare student widths while matching the regularization strength.
rows.value: same test error for κ ≫ 1 as for κ = 1
rows.note: The theorem is stated to make the global-minimum properties independent of network width for m ≥ d, given matched regularization; this reports no fall-rise-fall width curve in that regime.
rows.check: Not a width sweep. It is a consequence of Theorem 1 that results are independent of m for m≥d once regularization is rescaled (λ̃=λ/√κ), so the training recipe changes with width. It covers only κ≥1, a regime already past full capacity. Narrow students (κ<1), where a model-wise peak would sit, are not characterized. 'Absent' means no change of test error with width in that regime, not that a tested peak was missing.

rows.subject: two-layer quadratic neural network (ERM)

rows.locator: Section 4, Figure 3 center panel; interpolation-threshold discussion
rows.note: The text identifies the cusp in test error with the double-descent peak and says it appears in the region where the non-regularized training loss reaches zero.
rows.check: Figure-only, with no numeric peak height. The text says the cusp height at interpolation is finite under the PSD constraint and gives an analytic prediction for it. The baseline should be the test error on either side of α_inter (Result 1), or the larger-λ curves.

relationships.condition: Quadratic two-layer ERM, κ=m/d≥1, regularization rescaled with width
relationships.reason: Test error is exactly width-independent for κ≥1 (r1). There is no further descent from widening once m≥d, and the peak-location regime κ<1 is not characterized.
relationships.display_finding: Test error was exactly independent of width for κ≥1 under width-rescaled regularization.

source_check.reason: Width independence for κ≥1 establishes saturation within this regime, without testing the model-size sweep across the interpolation threshold required by V1. The untested threshold regime cannot justify limits_scope.

relationships.condition: Noisy (Δ=0.5, κ*=0.2) quadratic-network ERM, λ→0+, sample ratio sweep
relationships.reason: A test-error cusp, called the double-descent peak, sits where non-regularized training loss reaches zero (r2). Appendix G (Fig 5, no PSD constraint, from the text) reports test error diverging at α=0.5.
relationships.display_finding: Test error has a cusp where unregularized training loss reaches zero, and diverges at α=0.5 without the positive-semidefinite constraint.
